newsitem.title: UK: Drop in UK November PPI need not mean lower RPIs.
newsitem.headline: Drop in UK November PPI need not mean lower RPIs.

text.p: An unexpectedly large drop in UK producer input prices provides welcome further evidence that inflationary pressures are subdued, but it will not necessarily be matched by softer retail prices, economists said.
"Not only were output prices more benign than expectations but we had a phenomenal drop in input costs as well on the month," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Discount.
"We should see output price inflation contained over the next few months, but I would be a little more hesitant to extend that to the retail price level."
Shaw noted that the output price environment had been very benign since the start of the year but the out-turn for underlying inflation (RPIX) had nevertheless been disappointing.
RPIX jumped to 3.3 percent year-on-year in October. November figures are due on Thursday.

Producer input prices fell a seasonally adjusted 3.2 percent in November from the previous month and were down 5.5 percent year-on-year. Output prices were unchanged on the month and up 2.1 percent year-on-year.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International Europe, also noted the contrast between PPI and RPIX.
"There is something...driving a wedge between output prices and retail prices and I think the answer is an expansion of retail margins," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"This won't translate directly into good retail prices."
Part of the fall in input prices was due to a reversal of recent rises in oil prices. They fell around five percent in November from October, says Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets.

"Virtually all of the other components also made a negative contribution, with the recent strength of sterling clearly working to keep raw material costs under tight control right across the board," he said.

On the output side, Loynes noted that the core rate -- excluding food, drink, tobacco and petrol -- fell to 0.8 percent in November, a 30-year low. He expects it to nudge down further in the next month or two.

"If, as we expect, a recovery in manufacturing output prompts a rebound in productivity growth, then wage costs growth should slow sharply next year, helping to keep output price inflation under control throughout 1997."
Loynes takes a more optimistic view of the outlook, arguing that core output price inflation should feed through into retail prices despite the widening of retail margins.

Economists said the data did not significantly alter the outlook for interest rates but would strengthen Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's hand in resisting higher rates if Bank of England Governor Eddie George should call for a tightening at Wednesday's monetary meeting.
"This should reassure markets that there is no need for rate rises at the moment," economists at Royal Bank of Scotland commented.
"This meeting has been preceded by comments from the Chancellor and Governor which suggest no rate move before Christmas."
Shaw said the PPI numbers would "make life a little easier for the chancellor if he wants to fend off calls for higher interest rates on Wednesday."

"With a rather volatile political situation, both the chancellor and the prime minister may decide that it would be politically inappropriate to see rates going up now. But I still wouldn't completely rule it out."
